'''Central Avenue''' is a 12-block-long thoroughfare in the [[Jersey City Heights|Heights]] neighborhood of [[Jersey City, New Jersey]], United States.<ref name=HobokenGirl>{{cite web|url=https://www.hobokengirl.com/jersey-city-heights-historical-walking-tour/|author=Gittleman, Nicole|title=A Historical Walking Tour of Jersey City Heights|publisher=The Hoboken Girl|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=January 10, 2023|access-date=January 19, 2023|archive-date=January 11, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230111171946/https://www.hobokengirl.com/jersey-city-heights-historical-walking-tour/}}</ref> One of 13 shopping districts in the city,<ref name=JCShopping>{{cite web|url=http://www.jerseycityonline.com/jersey_city_shopping_districts.htm|title=Jersey City Shopping Districts|language=en-US|url-status=live|date=2007|access-date=January 19, 2023|archive-date=January 19, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230119143636/http://www.jerseycityonline.com/jersey_city_shopping_districts.htm}}</ref> it is designated '''County Route 663''' for {{convert|1.60|mi|km|2|adj=on}} of its length. It originates at the intersection of [[Summit Avenue (Hudson Palisades)|Summit Avenue]] and Pavonia Avenue, and runs north, intersecting [[Newark Plank Road|Newark Avenue]] one block east of [[Five Corners, Jersey City|Five Corners]] to [[Paterson Plank Road]] near [[Transfer Station, Hudson County|Transfer Station]]. The avenue continues north through [[Union City, New Jersey|Union City]] without the county route designation to 35th Street (CR 674<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.state.nj.us/transportation/refdata/sldiag/09000674__-.pdf|format=PDF|title=Hudson County 674 straight line diagram|publisher=[[New Jersey Department of Transportation]]|accessdate=2009-08-25|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017201306/http://www.state.nj.us/transportation/refdata/sldiag/09000674__-.pdf|archive-date=2012-10-17}}</ref>), two blocks north of [[Hackensack Plank Road]].<ref>{{Cite book|publisher = Hagstrom Map Company, Inc|isbn=0-88097-763-9|title=Hudson County New Jersey Street Map|year=2008}}</ref>

==History==
Central Avenue was the "Main Street" of [[Hudson City, New Jersey|Hudson City]],<ref name=HobokenGirl/><ref name=NJ.com>Strunsky, Steve (October 25, 2010). [http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2010/10/holland_tunnel_commuters_face.html "Holland Tunnel commuters face 5 years of added delays"]. [[NJ.com]].</ref> one of the municipalities which elected to join Jersey City in a referendum held in 1863. The avenue begins at what had been the southern border of the town that is now near the [[county seat]] of [[Hudson County]] and the historic [[Hudson County Courthouse]]. Traveling north it almost immediately passes over three man-made ravines, or "[[Cut (earthmoving)|cuts]]" through the part of the [[Hudson Palisades]] called [[Bergen Hill]]. The now-unused [[Bergen Arches]] and the single track [[Long Dock Tunnel]] were created for railroads, while [[New Jersey Route 139|The Depressed Highway]]<ref name=NJ.com/> (the bridge over which was replaced in 2017)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nj.com/jjournal-news/2017/05/central_avenue_bridge_reopens.html|title=Central Avenue bridge reopens in Jersey City|author=Villanova, Patrick|publisher=[[NJ.com]]|date=May 8, 2017|accessdate=August 15, 2021|archive-date=August 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210815111150/https://www.nj.com/jjournal-news/2017/05/central_avenue_bridge_reopens.html}}</ref> was created to allow traffic to by-pass local roads while travelling between the [[Holland Tunnel]] and the [[Pulaski Skyway]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/pages/p_pages/pulaski_skyway.htm |title= General Casimir Pulaski Memorial Skyway |work= Jersey City Past and Present|publisher=[[New Jersey City University]]|first1=Carmela|last1=Karnoutsos|first2= Patrick|last2=Shalhoub|year=2007|accessdate=October 1, 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20101001030230/http://www.njcu.edu/Programs/jchistory/Pages/P_Pages/Pulaski_Skyway.htm |archive-date= 2010-10-01 |url-status= dead }}</ref> In July 2012, the [[Hudson County Board of Chosen Freeholders]] passed a resolution to extend the avenue between Hoboken Avenue and Newark Avenue.<ref>Machcinski, Anthony J. (August 11, 2012). [http://www.nj.com/jjournal-news/index.ssf/2012/08/hudson_freeholders_want_to_ext.html "Hudson Freeholders want to extend Jersey City's Central Avenue near courthouse"]. NJ.com</ref><ref>{{cite news|last = Machcinski|first =  Anthony J|title = Set on extending Central Avenue in Jersey City, freeholders plan to take action to acquire property|publisher=NJ.com|newspaper = The Jersey Journal|date = October 23, 2012|url = http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2012/10/resolution_to_acquire_property.html|accessdate = 2013-03-09}}</ref> The work would be done in conjunction with the replacement of the [[Hudson County Administration Building]] with a new courthouse. Land for the new building had been acquired by the end of 2017. In September 2018, allocations for design of the site were made, with construction planned for 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nj.com/hudson/2018/09/project_to_build_new_hudson_county_justice_complex.html|publisher=[[NJ.com]]|title=Project to build new Hudson County justice complex finally making strides|author=Conte, Michaelangelo|date=September 18, 2018|accessdate=August 15, 2021|archive-date=September 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926125812/https://www.nj.com/hudson/2018/09/project_to_build_new_hudson_county_justice_complex.html}}</ref>

==Geography and commerce==
Central Avenue is one of Jersey City's 13 different neighborhood shopping districts.<ref name=JCShopping/> with more than 240 businesses serving the area.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jcheights.com/community-aboutJCHeights.shtml|title=The Heights Section of Jersey City|publisher=Central Avenue Special Improvement District|language=en-US|url-status=live|access-date=March 10, 2019|archive-date=December 31, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191231172831/http://www.jcheights.com/community-aboutJCHeights.shtml}}</ref> On entering the Heights, it becomes residential for a few blocks, as it passes the [[Jersey City Reservoir No. 3|Jersey City Reservoir #3]] and [[Pershing Field]]. Thereafter it becomes{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} a local shopping street.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cityofjerseycity.com/visitor.aspx?id=840|title=Shopping|publisher=The Official Jersey City Web Site|date=2007|archive-date=August 23, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130823114323/http://www.cityofjerseycity.com/visitor.aspx?id=840}}</ref> Businesses, retail and food shops are mostly located in three and four story buildings, many built in the late 19th and early 20th century. It again becomes more residential as it approaches the city line in Washington Park.{{citation needed|date=July 2012}}

The trajectory of the avenue is adjusted by a short "dog-leg turn" to the west along [[Paterson Plank Road]] and resumes in Union City. It is a broad residential street of multiple family houses and low and mid-rise apartment buildings. At 18th Street, the avenue is once again "interrupted", this time at the grounds of the former [[Monastery and Church of Saint Michael the Archangel]]. It continues on the other side and soon thereafter passes over the [[New Jersey Route 495|Lincoln Tunnel Approach and Helix]]. Central Avenue ends two blocks north of the 32nd Street section of the [[Hackensack Plank Road]] near the Holy Family Church complex, which includes the [[Park Performing Arts Center|Park Theater]], just west of [[Bergenline Avenue]].{{citation needed|date=March 2013}}
